title: Meta Launches Muse Code, Its First AI Coding Agent, in Challenge to Anthropic and OpenAI
excerpt: The new agent, built on the freshly released Muse Spark 1.2, offers a feedback tier at 20 cents per million output tokens—a fraction of competitors' pricing that could reshape the coding agent market.
body:
• Meta launched Muse Code on Wednesday, its first dedicated AI coding agent, entering a market dominated by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex with an aggressive pricing strategy.
  • Muse Code offers two tiers: a standard tier matching the Muse Spark model's pricing, and a feedback tier at just 20 cents per million output tokens—less than one-tenth the standard cost—for users who agree to provide improvement data.
  • The agent is built on Muse Spark 1.2, released the same day, which extends Meta's proprietary AI model family that began with Muse Spark 1.1 in July and marks a shift from the company's historically open-source approach.
  • The launch comes as Meta faces investor pressure to demonstrate returns on AI spending, with shares down 10% last week after CEO Mark Zuckerberg declined to detail the company's cloud computing plans during an earnings call.

Entering a Crowded Arena

Meta Platforms has released its first AI coding agent, called Muse Code, directly challenging Anthropic and OpenAI in one of the fastest-growing segments of the AI industry.

https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2084748111239344556

Coding agents—AI tools that can autonomously write, debug, and deploy software with minimal human intervention—have become a primary battleground in the AI race. Anthropic's Claude Code, launched in December, was credited with powering the company to a leading position in enterprise AI adoption. OpenAI followed with Codex. Meta's entry arrives months behind both but pitches itself as the low-cost alternative.

"We think that for a lot of workflows and a lot of use cases, this can be an incredibly good option, especially from a cost perspective."

— Alexandr Wang, Meta's Chief AI Officer

Wang said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal that some Meta employees are already using Muse Code internally and that he expects adoption to ramp up across the company.

The Price War Strategy

Muse Code's most notable feature is its pricing structure. The agent offers two distinct tiers. The standard tier charges the same rates as Meta's Muse Spark model—$1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, according to Reuters.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=AOvdJldBHCA

The second, more aggressive tier drops the output cost to just 20 cents per million tokens. The catch: users on this tier must agree to provide feedback that helps Meta improve the agent. In an industry where output token costs from competitors range from $10 per million (Claude Sonnet 5) to $30 per million (GPT-5.6 Sol), the feedback tier represents a radical pricing experiment.

Claude Code and Codex are typically bundled in subscription plans costing roughly $20 per month, with pay-as-you-go rates kicking in above usage caps. Meta's approach skips the subscription model entirely, betting that raw per-token pricing will attract developers who want predictable costs at scale.

Built on Muse Spark 1.2

Muse Code runs on Muse Spark 1.2, the latest version of Meta's proprietary AI model, also released on Wednesday. The Muse Spark family represents a significant strategic shift for Meta, which had previously built its AI reputation on the open-source Llama model series.

Muse Spark 1.1, launched on July 9, was the first model from Meta's Superintelligence Labs to be offered through a paid API. It was positioned as a multimodal reasoning model with strengths in coding, tool use, and agentic tasks. CEO Mark Zuckerberg broke a three-year silence on X to promote the original launch, calling it "a strong agentic and coding model at a very low price."

The 1.2 update appears to extend those capabilities specifically for the Muse Code agent, though Meta has not published detailed benchmark comparisons between the two versions.

The Investor Pressure

The launch arrives amid mounting pressure on Meta to show concrete returns from its AI investments. Shares in the company fell 10% last week following a quarterly earnings call in which Zuckerberg declined to provide new details about discussions around establishing a cloud-computing service—a potential revenue stream that investors have been watching closely.

Meta's capital expenditure on AI infrastructure has been among the highest in the industry, and each new product release is scrutinized for its potential to generate revenue beyond advertising. Muse Code, with its pay-per-use model and enterprise-facing positioning, represents a direct attempt to build a commercial AI business alongside Meta's core social media operations.

What It Means for Developers

For the global developer community—particularly the large Indian engineering workforce that contributes to both Meta's internal teams and the broader AI ecosystem—Muse Code offers a new option in the coding agent market. The feedback tier's extreme low pricing could be particularly attractive for startups and smaller development teams in India, where cost sensitivity shapes tool adoption decisions.

The competitive dynamics are shifting quickly. With Google overhauling its AI leadership on the same day, Anthropic expanding its enterprise offerings, and now Meta entering the coding agent arena at aggressive price points, developers have more choices—and more leverage—than at any point in the AI era.
